brief:
# Brief: a 4K HDR film with a burned-in subtitle does not play on the dogfood (JS-154)

Figures and commands: `~/.cache/jellyscale/po/js154-measurements.md`. "Unverified" marks every claim nothing measured.

**What viewers have today.** On the dogfood, a 4K HDR or Dolby Vision film that has to be re-encoded (an SDR screen or a browser that cannot play it as it is, or a PGS subtitle to draw into the picture) is made at 0.56 to 0.63 times real time. The film starts, then stalls and keeps stalling. No message says why. Three plays did this on 2026-11-20 (jobs 82, 83, 85).

**Why.** Three causes, each measured:

1. **The dogfood's processor cannot do this job in real time, with or without the subtitle.** On its own CPU (a 4-core i5-6500, measured in a pod on that node), decoding the 4K picture uses 2.1 cores, tone mapping it to SDR 1.0, encoding 0.4 to 0.6, and drawing the subtitle 0 to 0.1. In all, 3.8 to 4.1 cores for each second of film. The node gives the server 4 cores and its other pods use about 1 of them. Decoding and tone mapping alone already run at 0.83 to 1.0 times real time. **The burn-in is not the cause.** The same film without a subtitle measured the same (0.84 to 0.86x), so every 4K HDR re-encode on the dogfood stalls.
2. **The price is wrong for this machine.** The server prices this job at 3.2 cores. That figure was measured on a much faster 16-thread machine, where the same job does use 2.3 to 2.4 cores. A "core" in the price is a core of that machine. The dogfood's cores do about 1.6 times less work each.
3. **Sharing across the cluster cannot happen with one worker.** Helpers (other workers making chunks of the film ahead of the viewer) start only on another worker, and only when one has room for the job's full price plus room left for a new viewer. The dogfood runs a single worker, so no helper can ever start. The code works as written here. The cluster has 22 processors (nodes of 12, 6 and 4) and the server uses the smallest node's 4.

**Is BL-100 this one?** Probably not. BL-100 is a stall in a test scenario on the test stack's small fixture films ("timed out waiting for playback past 22"), traced to a job-waiting path (Jobs.segment and catchUpSegments). The dogfood failure is the processor's speed. Their mechanisms are unrelated from what the docs say. It is unverified whether that test scenario ever ran slower than real time.

**The measuring pod ran faster than the dogfood did.** On the same CPU, a measuring pod ran today's job at 0.81 to 0.87x where the dogfood's own jobs ran at 0.56 to 0.63x, so real conditions were about 0.7 of the pod's. Why is unverified: other films, the server's own work in the same 4 cores, or a subtitle extraction running alongside. The lead can read the job rows to settle it. **Every figure below that was measured in the pod may be about 0.7 times as fast in the dogfood's own pod.**

**Who is affected, how often.** Every viewer whose client cannot take a 4K HDR or Dolby Vision film as it is, and every viewer who picks a PGS subtitle that the client does not draw itself. jellyfin-web leaves PGS drawing off by default, so in practice every jellyfin-web viewer who turns such a subtitle on. Every such play on the dogfood fails. How many plays that is: unverified. JS-153's decision counters will count them.

## Options

Each option is priced in what the viewer gets, what the owner changes, and what it costs to build. Several can be combined.

**A. The film plays in real time on the dogfood by sharing it across the cluster (helpers).**
- *Viewer:* the film plays at 1080p, tone mapped, subtitle drawn, as promised, if the helpers together reach real time. The first seconds still come from the viewer's own job at about 0.85x (0.6x on the dogfood).
- *How many helpers the server allows:* a helper goes only where it leaves room for another job of the same price somewhere. With two more 4-core workers like the dogfood's, **one** helper runs, about 1.7x in total from pod figures (about 1.2x scaled to the dogfood's 0.6x; unverified end to end). A 12-processor worker allows two helpers on it. Their speed is unverified, because that node's CPU was not measured. A 6-processor worker alone allows none.
- *Needs:* more workers. The dogfood would run a worker role on a second node, k3s-master (12 processors, nearly idle, about 0.4 cores used) or k3s-worker2 (6 processors). That is an owner homelab change: another Deployment or pod with the worker role, the library mounted, the same Postgres and transcode store. The dogfood's transcode store is `file:///data` on a ReadWriteOnce volume, so a second worker would need a shared store (S3 or similar). That is a bigger change, and unverified as the only path. A higher price (option D) raises the room every helper needs with it.
- *Build:* likely none in jellyscale for the sharing itself. The job's price should still match the machine (see D), otherwise the viewer's own worker stays overbooked.
- *Leaves:* a seek still lands on a slow job until helpers catch up (unverified how long).

**B. The iGPU on the dogfood's node (a first hardware slice, BL-040).**
- *What the dogfood's iGPU can do (measured):* the HD 530 (Skylake) **cannot decode 10-bit HEVC**, so the CPU still decodes every 4K HDR film (2.1 cores). Its video processor cannot tone map either. It can tone map through OpenCL and encode H.264.
- *Viewer, measured in a pod on that node:* CPU decode, iGPU tone map (OpenCL) and iGPU encode ran at 1.09x. CPU decode, Jellyfin's faster CPU tone map and iGPU encode ran at 1.10 to 1.12x. That is barely over real time, below the 1.2x the server asks for margin. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap (about 0.7), it is about 0.77x, so it is **not shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod**. A seek or a second viewer would stall it, and the node's other pods take the margin. The iGPU encode needed far more bitrate for the same picture at the settings tried, 31 times on a dark scene. A quality-targeted mode was not tried, so the bitrate it would need is unverified.
- *Needs:* the owner gives the pod the GPU (`gpu.intel.com/i915: 1`, the cluster's device plugin, as Jellyfin already has; no privileged container). The image needs the Intel VA driver, plus OpenCL or jellyfin-ffmpeg for the tone map; Alpine's ffmpeg has neither the OpenCL runtime nor `tonemapx` today (unverified for the Alpine packages). The build is a new encode path with its own checks (detection, fallback to CPU, a price per machine).
- *Better hardware in the same cluster:* the other two nodes have newer iGPUs (UHD 630, Coffee Lake and Comet Lake). Those are generally documented to decode 10-bit HEVC and tone map in hardware, which would take most of the CPU load away (**unverified; not measured**). A first slice on those nodes means the worker runs there, which is option A's homelab change too.

**C. A cheaper output when the job is this heavy.**
- *x264 ultrafast in place of veryfast:* 0.91x on the dogfood's CPU. **Does not reach real time.** Same picture at 3.2 times the bytes. Not an option on its own.
- *720 lines in place of 1080:* 1.04 to 1.11x in the pod on the dogfood's CPU, with no margin. With Jellyfin's faster tone map it reached 1.22x, but that needs jellyfin-ffmpeg in the image. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap: about 0.75x and 0.85x, so **neither is shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod**. *The viewer loses* 56% of the pixels: softer detail and softer subtitle edges on a large screen. On the dark test scene the measured loss was small (SSIM 0.9911 against 0.9919), and on a detailed scene it would be larger (unverified). D-038 already says an output below 1080 lines is a loss needing this brief. This option breaks the 1080-line ceiling's promise of 1080 for these films.
- *Build:* a rule for when to drop to 720 (by machine speed, not by film), and its checks.

**D. Price the job by what it costs on the worker, so a play the worker cannot hold is refused within seconds with a reason.**
- *Viewer:* instead of a film that starts and stalls, a "cannot be played at this time" message within seconds, and the log names the reason (`cores are short`, with the cost). Nothing plays.
- *What it does on the dogfood:* the measured cost on its CPU is 3.8 to 4.1 cores. A play is refused only when the price is **above the worker's declared cores**. The dogfood declares none and gets 4. A price of 3.9 still fits and still stalls. Above 4.0 it is refused, provided the floor that lets a default worker take the dearest job alone (3.2 today) is not raised with the price, or the dogfood declares fewer cores than the price. Then **every 4K HDR re-encode is refused**, burn-in or not, on every client that cannot take the film as it is. The dogfood worker then holds no such job at all. Today it holds one, which stalls, beside one 1080p SDR re-encode.
- *Elsewhere:* the price is one number for every machine. Raised to 4.1 everywhere, a 16-core worker holds 3 such films instead of 5, although on a fast machine the job uses 2.4 cores. A price per worker, measured or declared by its speed, avoids that. It is a bigger build (unverified size).
- D-038 already ruled this a floor, not the closer. It also fixes the silent stall, and it pairs with A, B or C.

**E. Keep today's behaviour.** The film starts and stalls on the dogfood. A viewer gets no reason. Listed for completeness. It breaks "playback never surprises a viewer" and "every failure is reported with its reason".

## Facts the decision may turn on

- The cause is CPU speed for 4K HDR on one 4-core i5-6500, not the subtitle. Whatever is chosen applies to every 4K HDR re-encode on the dogfood, not only burn-ins.
- In the measuring pod on the dogfood's node, only 720 lines with jellyfin-ffmpeg's tone map cleared 1.2x (1.22x), and the iGPU options cleared 1.0x but not 1.2x. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap, none of them is shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod.
- Measured: the dogfood's 4-core node, alone or with its iGPU. Not measured: the 12- and 6-processor nodes' CPUs and their newer iGPUs, and helpers end to end. Options A and B on those nodes rest on unmeasured figures, and they change the owner's homelab: another worker, a shared transcode store, the GPU in the pod.
- Any homelab change (another worker, the GPU in the pod) goes to the owner before it is made.

## Added by the lead
- Why the dogfood ran at 0.56-0.63x where the measurement pod ran at 0.81-0.87x: the dogfood's own log (2026-11-20 22:14:54) shows "image track extraction started" for the same film at the same moment as job 82 (the PGS track read from a 46.7 GB file, BL-234), on the same 4 cores. So on the dogfood a burn-in costs the re-encode plus a concurrent whole-file read; without a subtitle the stall would be the pod's 0.85x.
- Unmeasured: k3s-master (Comet Lake, 12 CPUs, nearly idle; UHD 630, which as a generation decodes HEVC Main10 in hardware and has VPP tone mapping) and k3s-worker2 (Coffee Lake, 6 CPUs, UHD 630). Running the dogfood's worker there, or a second worker there, is a homelab change the owner decides; measuring there first is the same kind of temporary pod the owner approved for k3s-worker1.
tradeoff: JS-154 measured: the dogfood's 4-core i5-6500 needs 3.8 to 4.1 CPU-seconds per second of any 4K HDR re-encode (priced 3.2 on a machine 1.6 times faster per core), so it runs at about 0.85x and stalls, burn-in or not; decode and tone mapping are the cost; the HD 530 cannot decode Main 10 or tone map in hardware (1.1x in a quiet pod at 31 times the bytes); one worker gets no helper. Given up, by dogfood viewers, until a second worker runs: every 4K HDR or Dolby Vision re-encode is refused with a reason instead of played. Given up by every deployment: a bounded speed measurement at each worker start, fewer viewers on slow machines than the docs promised, and a default worker that no longer takes the dearest job alone. Unverified when decided: helpers end to end, the other two nodes' CPUs and iGPUs, that a declared transcodeCores of 3 refuses the job. The lead read from the dogfood's log that the PGS extraction started beside jobs 82 and 85, and job 83 within its run.
entry: The price table stays one, in cores of a named reference machine; a worker's capacity is measured on the worker at start, not declared, and a play no worker holds at real time is refused within seconds with its reason (JS-161, taking BL-005). That is the floor. The closer is a second worker sharing or holding the film, the product as PRODUCT.md describes it: JS-162 measures helpers end to end in jellyfin-web on 2-CPU workers, JS-163 measures the other two nodes, and their briefs decide whether anything is built. Rejected: 720 lines (a picture loss not shown to reach real time), a hardware slice on the HD 530, one raised global price, today's silent stall. BL-040 stays in the backlog, re-pointed at the UHD 630 nodes. JS-135 prices in reference cores and depends on JS-161; JS-136 and JS-148 depend on JS-161 in place of JS-154. JS-154 closes with its record in docs/transcoding.md. Order: superseded by D-045. Data that reopens it: JS-162 showing helpers do not reach real time as built; JS-163 showing a UHD 630 holds the job at 1.2x at no more than twice x264's bytes.
serves: PRODUCT.md goal 1: Playback never surprises a viewer; 'A heavy film uses the whole cluster's processors rather than stalling on one machine while others sit idle'; 'Growing is adding machines'; 'every failure is reported with its reason, never silent'; 'Operating it stays boring'.
